resolver_cross_check.purpose: verify that a real fresh install emits the lsblk -s crypt chain parsed by lib-luks-identity.sh:48-49
resolver_cross_check.result: FALSE PASS, NOW CORRECTED TO FAIL. The original entry read 'PASS - the discovery risk carried since round 3 is retired'. It captured the CONTENT of the lsblk -s chain correctly (fedora_hermes-root lvm / luks-8919c2b1-... crypt / nvme0n1p3 part / nvme0n1 disk) but never reproduced the EXACT BYTE OUTPUT. util-linux 2.41.5 prefixes that tree with box-drawing glyphs, so the real chain reads 'fedora_hermes-root lvm / <glyph>luks-8919c2b1-... crypt / <glyph>nvme0n1p3 part / <glyph>nvme0n1 disk', and lib-luks-identity.sh:48-49 field-parsed NAME with awk, producing a glyph-prefixed mapper name. Discovery therefore FAILED on the real host when tpm-enroll.sh --preflight was first run. The lesson generalises: confirming that a tool's output CONTAINS the expected data is not the same as confirming that the parser handles the output the tool actually EMITS.

dns_resolution.question: does hermes.ai.lab.local resolve, and is the guide's 5.5 'update the workstation's host entry and confirm it resolves' necessary or merely convenient?
dns_resolution.router_record_is_correct: YES. Both router interfaces answer authoritatively: dig +short @10.0.30.254 hermes.ai.lab.local and dig +short @192.168.99.254 hermes.ai.lab.local each return 10.0.30.10, with status NOERROR, ANSWER 1 and TTL 86400. Reverse lookup of 10.0.30.10 returns hermes.ai.lab.local. The DHCP network for VLAN 30 is configured with domain=ai.lab.local, which is where the name comes from. NETWORK_DESIGN.md is therefore accurate: the record exists.
dns_resolution.workstation_stub_resolver_fails: YES, and the cause is structural, not a misconfiguration of the router. Queries through the workstation's systemd-resolved stub (127.0.0.53) fail: dig hermes.ai.lab.local returns status REFUSED with dig's own warning '.local is reserved for Multicast DNS', and resolvectl query hermes.ai.lab.local returns 'resolve call failed: No appropriate name servers or networks for name found'. Resolving the same name directly against the router succeeds, which isolates the failure to the client's resolver path rather than to DNS data.
dns_resolution.root_cause: the lab domain ai.lab.local ends in the reserved mDNS TLD .local (RFC 6762). systemd-resolved routes any name under .local to multicast DNS and refuses to send it to unicast DNS servers. On this workstation resolvectl status eno1 shows '-mDNS', so mDNS is disabled as well - the name therefore has no route at all: not unicast (reserved) and not multicast (disabled). This is why NETWORK_DESIGN.md records 'resolution failed from the audit workstation; validate the resolver path before relying on it', and why AGENTS.md instructs using the verified IP 10.0.30.10.
dns_resolution.blast_radius: every unicast name in the lab under .local is affected, not just this host - mgmt.lab.local and ai.lab.local behave the same way (dig returns REFUSED through the stub and empty for router.mgmt.lab.local), while direct queries to the router work. Any Linux client running systemd-resolved will behave this way.
dns_resolution.consequence_for_5_5: the guide's instruction is not a formality: the workstation hosts entry is the ONLY thing that will make the name resolve there, because the DNS path cannot carry a .local name. Choosing the static hostname hermes.ai.lab.local is still correct - it matches the DNS record, the DHCP-derived transient name and NETWORK_DESIGN.md - but name resolution must come from /etc/hosts on each client, not from DNS.
dns_resolution.recommendation: structural fix, outside gate B6: rename the lab domain away from the reserved .local TLD (for example ai.lab.internal or ai.lab.arpa) so unicast DNS can serve it, or keep .local and accept per-client /etc/hosts entries. A narrower alternative worth testing on the workstation is an explicit routing domain, resolvectl domain eno1 '~ai.lab.local', which may override the mDNS special-casing for that suffix; it was NOT tested here because it needs root on the workstation.

the deployment guide phase 5.4 says to 'review /etc/dnf/automatic.conf and set staging', but that file does not exist on a fresh Fedora 44 install even after dnf5-plugin-automatic is installed. RESOLVED on inspection, and the guide's PATH is correct: dnf5-automatic(8) states 'Default values are set from /usr/share/dnf5/dnf5-plugins/automatic.conf ... Host-specific overrides from /etc/dnf/automatic.conf are then applied', and rpm -qlv confirms /etc/dnf/automatic.conf is a zero-byte %ghost placeholder that the package declares but never creates. The residual defect is the WORD 'review', which implies an existing file to read; a fresh install has nothing to review and the operator must create the override. Two confusions sit alongside it: a second ghost, /etc/dnf/dnf5-plugins/automatic.conf, is also declared and also absent, and the plugin binary carries the string 'Warning: Configuration file location "{}" for dnf automatic is deprecated. See dnf5-automatic(8) for details', so one of the two locations is deprecated and writing the wrong one could be a silent no-op. The documented override path is the one to use. Separately, the shipped defaults in /usr/share/dnf5/dnf5-plugins/automatic.conf already match the guide's intent (apply_updates = no, download_updates = yes, upgrade_type = default, reboot = never, emit_via = stdio), so this step pins behaviour that is already the default rather than changing it - which is a real benefit, because an override file prevents a future package update to the shipped default from silently switching the host to auto-applying updates.

PCR7 is readable WITHOUT root from /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/pcr-sha256/7 (mode 444), even though tpm2_pcrread sha256:7 fails for aicowork because /dev/tpm0 and /dev/tpmrm0 are mode 0600. This is an opportunity rather than a defect: the agent can verify PCR7 directly over ssh without privilege, and should use the sysfs path for verification while reserving tpm2_pcrread for console confirmation. a fourth independent machine discriminator exists and the agent misused it once: the two machines have different PCR7 values (server 22103EAC..., workstation EF99FE48...) because PCR7 measures the Secure Boot policy state of that specific firmware. The agent read /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/pcr-sha256/7 in its own workstation shell and briefly compared the WORKSTATION's value against the SERVER's pre-reboot value, producing an apparent PCR7 change across the reboot that was purely an artifact of reading the wrong machine. This is the same wrong-machine failure mode as the operator incidents in operator_hazards, committed by the agent. Rule: every PCR7 or device-path read must be confirmed to originate on the intended host, for example by echoing hostname in the same command; when read locally rather than over ssh it is the workstation's value.

a reporting trap worth knowing for replication: systemctl show -p <PathAssertOrCondition> returns EMPTY even when the directive is present and correctly applied, because this systemd exposes only the aggregate ConditionResult, AssertResult and their timestamps as D-Bus properties, not the individual path-based directives. The correct way to verify a drop-in was loaded is systemctl show -p DropInPaths plus a property the drop-in does expose, such as RequiresMountsFor, and to confirm the directive is documented with 'man systemd.unit' and that systemd-analyze verify is clean. Without the comparison against lastlog2-import.service this would have been recorded as a false finding that the guide's mount guard was inert.

AGENT BLOCK DEFECT - bash history expansion silently rewrote the guard's warning text. The host guards were written as echo "!! WRONG MACHINE ..." using double quotes. In an interactive bash shell '!' triggers history expansion, so '!!' expanded to the full text of the operator's previous command: it produced 'clear WRONG MACHINE ...' in one paste and 'exit WRONG MACHINE ...' in another. The guard still functioned, because the protection lives in the if condition rather than in the message, and the wrong-machine paste was correctly inert. But the messages were unreliable, and in the general case an expanded previous command could inject misleading text. FIX, applied to every subsequent block: use SINGLE quotes for guard messages, which suppress history expansion, and avoid '!' characters in pasted strings entirely. This is worth recording because host guards are exactly the code an operator pastes blindly, so their output must be trustworthy.

Each start relabels the tree to that container's MCS categories, so the long-running gateway then gets 'denied { lock }' on /opt/data/state.db-shm with a category mismatch (process c519,c720 vs file c253,c452, permissive=0). By contrast /home/hermes/transport, which genuinely IS shared by two containers, correctly uses ':z'. Fix: use ':z' for gateway-state in all three places. Matters because Phase 7 requires no new AVC denials and because lock denials on SQLite's WAL shared-memory file cause intermittent state-persistence failures rather than clean errors. That made it a NON-DURABLE fix, and m05-tests.sh allowlist-swap/allowlist-restore were about to re-trigger it. All six missed lines are now ':z' (C36), verified staged in the bundle by hash. The mechanism itself is now measured rather than inferred: ':Z' relabels the DIRECTORY to the container's private categories, and because every child inherits the directory's level, a single ':Z' mount re-stamps the entire tree.

m04-backup.sh:111-112 reports diff_rc from head, not diff. The script runs `diff -r /home/hermes/gateway-state "$RESTORE/home/hermes/gateway-state" 2>&1 | head -n 10` and then `echo "diff_rc=$?"`. In a pipeline `$?` is the status of the LAST command, and head returns 0 unconditionally, so diff_rc=0 is emitted no matter what diff found: the one check in the restore test that could have detected a bad archive cannot fail. The output is additionally truncated to 10 lines, which hid 3 of the 13 benign uv-cache symlink errors. A corrected re-run using `diff -rq --no-dereference` (comparing symlinks as symlinks) confirms the archive is faithful. The defect is not that the archive is bad - it is byte-faithful by hash - but that this check could never have said so, which is the same class as the corrected resolver_cross_check false PASS.

LATENT AND CREDENTIAL-DESTROYING - provision-telegram.sh:72 can silently wipe the gateway profile .env. The line is `grep -vE "^(TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN|TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS|TELEGRAM_ALLOW_ALL_USERS)=" /opt/data/.env > "$tmp" || true`. That grep is a READ of .env performed by a throwaway container carrying its own MCS categories. If the read is ever denied, grep exits 2, the `|| true` suppresses it, `set -e` on line 68 cannot fire BY CONSTRUCTION because `cmd || true` always succeeds, $tmp stays empty, and `mv -f` installs a THREE-LINE .env holding only the Telegram keys: OPENAI_API_KEY, the gateway-generated API_SERVER_KEY and the four hardening flags are gone. The only symptom would be env_lines=3 on line 79, while telegram_token_lines=1 on line 86 still reports success. Dormant on this host because the tree is uniformly container_file_t:s0 with no MCS suffix and an empty category set is a subset of every process's category set, so the read cannot be denied. Distinct from the provision-openai-key.sh truncation defect: that one clobbers unconditionally on every run, this one clobbers only via a security-denial path, and it reports success either way. Fix: drop the `|| true` and fail loudly when the filter cannot read the file.

scripts/hermes/manual/README.md:69 states the policy 'socket; everything else uses :Z (private)'. That is the rule the eight gateway-state ':Z' sites were written under, and it is wrong for any directory shared with a second container - it is the documentation defect behind the C31/C36 spread. The correct rule is by ownership rather than by default: ':z' for anything a second container also mounts, ':Z' only for a path owned by exactly one container, which is why worker-state/home, worker-state/ssh-host-keys and the four gateway-ssh binary mounts correctly keep ':Z'.

backup_path_review.confirmed_good: m04-backup.sh stops the writers before archiving (lines 60-62 stop hermes-gateway.service tolerantly and hermes-worker.service), creates the archive with tar --xattrs --acls --selinux inside a 0700 directory, restricts the archive and manifest to 0600, records sha256 values for the archive and for the gateway config, .env, worker host key and known_hosts as hashes rather than contents, performs a genuine isolated restore into /home/hermes/m04-restore-test-<ts>, and asserts the restored content by file counts, greps for 'backend: ssh', the model name and 'ssh_host: worker', and a diff -r of gateway-state. STEP 7 RESULT: both of the guide's acceptance criteria were met on the live host - entry counts 1524/1524, 450/450 and 11/11 exactly, and the three restored-config assertions returned 1, 3 and 1. It then removes the restored credential copy and verifies the removal, confirmed absent independently.
backup_path_review.minor_unasserted: the stopped state is recorded as 'worker_state=$(... is-active ...)' but never enforced, so a failed stop would let the archive proceed against live state. Same reports-but-does-not-assert pattern as fallback-wipe.sh and b4-verify.sh; low practical risk for these state files. CONFIRMED LIVE at step 7: the recorded value was worker_state=failed, which is the post-stop state of a Quadlet unit whose ExecStop removes the container, and the accompanying 'podman ps -a' printed nothing at all because there was no container left to list - so this line would not have distinguished a failed stop from a clean one either.
backup_path_review.diff_assertion_is_void: the 'diff -r' named in confirmed_good is not an assertion. m04-backup.sh:111-112 pipes diff into 'head -n 10' and then reads $?, which is head's status and is always 0. See known_instrument_defects. The restore test's real strength is the file counts and the three config greps; a corrected re-run with 'diff -rq --no-dereference' separately established that the archive is faithful.
backup_path_review.operational_notes: m04-backup.sh restarts only the worker. The gateway is stopped with a tolerated failure and returns through its Quadlet [Install] autostart at the next boot, which the m04 reboot sequence provides. CONFIRMED LIVE at step 7: after the helper finished, 'systemctl --user is-active hermes-gateway.service' returned inactive - a clean stop, not a failure - and exactly one conmon process remained, '-n hermes-worker'. SHARPEN: provision-telegram.sh does NOT restart the gateway, so it also stays down through the whole of step 8, and m05-telegram.sh:47 is the first thing that brings it back; any step-8 output therefore describes a host with the gateway stopped. The script stages the backup under /home/aicowork at 0700/0600 for off-disk transfer but does not perform the transfer itself; the archive contains the provider credential, so it must be pulled to private/hermes-app-backups/ on the LUKS-encrypted workstation and then deleted from the host. The archive's .env hash is a STOPPED-STATE value and goes stale the moment the gateway starts, because the gateway appends a generated API_SERVER_KEY to .env - see m04_step7_backup_and_restore. That does not affect restorability, because the key is regenerated when absent.

posture_path_review.confirmed_good: m04-posture.sh lists the credential files with ls -la so modes and sizes appear but never contents, and it reports removed duplicates by 16-character sha256 prefix only. The worker read-only probe is logically correct: a successful touch prints WRITABLE_UNEXPECTED, a failed one prints READONLY_OK. Removing the .env.pre-hardening-* duplicates and reinstalling the patched helper are real actions, not just checks.
posture_path_review.finding: the script is observation-only by design and its own header says so ('capture the effective runtime posture'), so unlike b4-verify.sh it does not misdescribe itself. The consequence stands anyway: M04's acceptance criteria - effective identity, capabilities, seccomp, SELinux, mounts and limits - are established solely by an operator reading printed output, with no machine-checkable pass or fail. Combined with verification_layer_gap, the M04 PASS recorded on the reference host rests on human reading rather than an enforced gate.
posture_path_review.unenforced_mutating_step: systemctl set-property "$SLICE" MemoryHigh=6G MemoryMax=8G TasksMax=1536 prints set_property_rc but never acts on it, so a failed budget application would still report success; the following systemctl show exposes the truth only to a reader
posture_path_review.coverage_asymmetry: the read-only root write probe runs inside hermes-worker only; the gateway ReadOnly=true is shown through podman inspect but never probed
posture_path_review.not_audited: m03-*.sh, m04-reboot.sh, m04-postboot.sh, m04-postboot-probe.sh and the m05-* scripts remain unaudited

readonly_gateway_review.finding: m04-readonly-gateway.sh is documented - in its own header lines 4-6 and in the guide's phase 6.3 sequence table at step 10 - as auto-reverting the unit 'if Telegram does not return'. The revert branch is gated only on systemd unit activity: line 90 tests [ "$gw_state" = active ] and line 108 is the else. A gateway that starts but never reaches Telegram is therefore accepted, and line 107 prints RESULT=PASS - read-only gateway root accepted while line 101 merely records telegram_connected_lines=$(telegram_state) without asserting it.
readonly_gateway_review.secondary: telegram_state() at lines 54-57 runs journalctl without -b, so it counts 'Connected to Telegram' across the last 200 lines irrespective of boot; a connection logged by an earlier run would keep the count non-zero and mask a current failure. b4-verify.sh:115 performs the equivalent check correctly with -b.
readonly_gateway_review.consequence: a read-only gateway rootfs that breaks Telegram while leaving the unit active stays installed and is reported as PASS, so the M04a acceptance evidence can read RESULT=PASS with a Telegram count of zero
readonly_gateway_review.fix: treat failure as (gw_state != active) OR (Telegram connection count for the current boot == 0), using journalctl -b as b4-verify.sh does, and revert in that case
readonly_gateway_review.confirmed_good: the pre-change unit backup to /root/hermes-gateway.container.pre-readonly-<ts> at mode 0600, the read-only probes against /, /run and /opt/data inside the gateway, the restorecon on the installed unit, and the explicit failure-journal dump in the revert branch

postboot_review.confirmed_good: m04-postboot-probe.sh handles a real SELinux trap explicitly and documents it better than anything else in the profile: its header explains that m04-postboot.sh installs m03-probe.py after the gateway has already started, that the :Z-mounted directory was labelled at container start, so the new file keeps the host default label and container_t is denied read. It relabels with chcon --reference against known_hosts and, if the first probe still fails, restarts the gateway so podman relabels the mount and retries.
postboot_review.finding: m04-postboot.sh is observation-only like the rest of the profile, and its central criterion has no mechanical check: it prints user_manager, linger, gateway, worker, podman ps and the container StartedAt values, but never compares StartedAt against the boot time, so 'both containers autostarted with no manual start' - the headline acceptance for gate B6 - is established by a human comparing timestamps. It also computes boot_changed=NO (unexpected) at lines 57-61 and takes no action on it.
postboot_review.ambiguity: m04-postboot.sh:83 reinstalls m03-probe.py and immediately re-runs it, which by the following script's own account produces an expected labelling failure, so the probe_rc it prints at that point is not meaningful. The script gives no indication that failure is expected here, so an operator reading only this output would reasonably conclude the transport is broken.
postboot_review.inconsistency_confirmed: m04-postboot.sh:77 scopes the Telegram check with journalctl -b, the same correct form used at b4-verify.sh:115. m04-readonly-gateway.sh's telegram_state() omits -b. Two of the three uses are correct, so that omission is an inconsistency rather than a house convention.
postboot_review.triage_note: m03-activate.sh, m03-configure-and-probe.sh, m04-reboot.sh, m05-fix-and-activate.sh, m05-gateway-diag.sh, m05-gateway-diag2.sh and m05-tests.sh were triaged by assertion-primitive count but not read line by line.

reboot_script_review.confirmed_good: m04-reboot.sh is the only script in the profile with an explicit human-confirmation gate for a destructive action: it warns that the LUKS passphrase is required at the console, requires the operator to type exactly 'REBOOT', and otherwise prints 'ABORTED - no reboot performed'. It also installs the gateway Quadlet with its [Install] section plus a restorecon, records boot_id, the is-enabled state of both units and the container StartedAt values, and runs sync before systemctl reboot. That is the right shape for a script whose purpose is to prepare a successful unattended boot.
reboot_script_review.fragility: the abort is correct but for a non-obvious reason: the 'exit 0' sits inside the '{ ... } | tee' group, so it terminates the subshell rather than the script. That does skip the systemctl reboot further down the same group, so the abort works, but because pipefail is not set and tee returns 0 the script still falls through to print WROTE=<file> as though it had completed normally. Relying on subshell scope to implement a safety abort is fragile.
reboot_script_review.pattern_again: like every other manual-profile script except the boot helpers it asserts nothing. A Quadlet missing its [Install] section would not stop it; gateway_enable_state and worker_enable_state are printed for a human, and the failure would first become visible after the reboot the script just performed.
reboot_script_review.audit_status: all scripts that perform a non-idempotent or safety-relevant action have now been read line by line. Still triaged only: m03-activate.sh, m03-configure-and-probe.sh, m05-fix-and-activate.sh, m05-gateway-diag.sh, m05-gateway-diag2.sh and m05-tests.sh.

application_gate_triage.method: counted assertion primitives (die, exit 1-9) and PASS/FAIL string emissions across every remaining script in scripts/hermes/manual/
application_gate_triage.result: no acceptance or verification script in the manual profile exits non-zero on a failed check. m03-activate.sh, m03-configure-and-probe.sh, m03-accept.sh, m04-reboot.sh, m04-postboot.sh, m04-postboot-probe.sh, m05-fix-and-activate.sh, m05-gateway-diag.sh and m05-gateway-diag2.sh contain no die and no exit statement at all. m05-tests.sh has four exits and every one is 'exit 2', the convention for usage errors rather than test failures. provision-worker-client-key.sh's four exits guard provisioning errors, which is appropriate for an action script.
application_gate_triage.sharpest_case: m03-accept.sh:103-113 runs the authenticated inference expecting exactly HERMES_OK and computes INFERENCE_RESULT=PASS or INFERENCE_RESULT=FAIL, then takes no action on FAIL - no exit, no revert, no downstream signal - and the script exits 0. inf_rc is captured and printed but is not part of the decision.

The point is that the guide's acceptance tables present these as gates with PASS/FAIL outcomes while no mechanical signal exists, so every application-phase gate's evidence is a human reading - the same conclusion as the rest of this section, now confirmed across the whole manual profile rather than a sample.

operator_hazards.machine_confusion: FOUR incidents, and the fourth is the most instructive. (1) The passphrase re-test ran on the workstation against its own /dev/nvme0n1p3 (UUID da58ecdb-...) and reported PASSPHRASE_OK for the wrong volume. (2) The authorized_keys install block was run on the workstation. (3) A guard using bare 'exit 1' was pasted into the operator's interactive shell, which closed the ssh session before the intended command ran. (4) The 5.5 pre-reboot capture and 'systemctl reboot' block was pasted into the WORKSTATION shell instead of the server, so the workstation rebooted unintentionally while the server was never rebooted. Root cause of (4) is a process failure on the agent's part, not operator carelessness: the verified_discriminator below already prescribed the guard, and the agent still issued a multi-machine step as an unguarded block after the operator had exited the server ssh session, leaving a workstation prompt that looks similar.
operator_hazards.verified_discriminator: the server's hostname is hermes.ai.lab.local and the workstation's is fedora, so a prefix test against hermes* separates them; both forms were tested. '/'home/hermes is a mountpoint' is an independent second check that is true only on the server. A guard intended for pasting into an interactive shell must not call exit, and should keep its actions inside an if-branch so the wrong machine does nothing rather than terminating the session.
operator_hazards.device_path_collision: both machines expose their LUKS container as /dev/nvme0n1p3, so any device-path command must be preceded by a cryptsetup luksUUID check: server 8919c2b1-5d9a-4fb9-8f85-97d286cbe7ec, workstation da58ecdb-2537-4b06-b794-10b8930b43c9.
operator_hazards.incident_4_impact: NIL, verified rather than assumed. The server was untouched - same boot_id 95d9c7ad-8c0d-4264-8635-ccdee6f572d7, uptime 37 minutes, static hostname hermes.ai.lab.local intact, 0 failed units - so the 5.5 reboot simply did not happen there. The workstation returned cleanly with 0 failed units, the repository and both evidence artifacts intact, and the /etc/hosts entry persisted across the reboot. Both off-host recovery backups were re-hashed after the reboot and match the recorded values exactly: header 8b4ca6884c4bc4c5a3ceba12266704e27fc2916d2d698a3f3fc2968c3e28e336 and crypttab f4b732ad0f9149139bae466a016e55287aa136c780e56cebe33ad9fe75dba43c. By-product: the unintended reboot is independent evidence that the workstation-side /etc/hosts change survives a reboot, which is exactly the persistence property 5.5 sets out to prove on the server.
operator_hazards.prevention_now_enforced: every remaining block is wrapped in a host guard that CONFIRMS the machine before acting: if [ "$(hostname)" != "hermes.ai.lab.local" ]; then echo WRONG MACHINE, nothing run; else <commands>; fi. The guard must not call exit - that was incident (3) - and keeps all actions inside the if-branch so a wrong-machine paste is inert. Workstation-only blocks are guarded symmetrically against hostname 'fedora'. Additionally each block opens by echoing the confirmed hostname and the operator is asked to check the shell prompt: the server prompt is 'aicowork@hermes:~$' and the workstation prompt is 'cloudops@fedora:...$'. Correction after a fifth wrong-machine paste: the guard's own message text was being rewritten by bash history expansion because it used double quotes around '!!'. Guards now use single quotes and no '!' characters, so the warning prints verbatim. The fifth paste landed on the workstation and was correctly inert, which is the guard doing its job on its first real test.

env_is_runtime_mutated_by_the_gateway.evidence: live .env was 318 bytes at mtime 21:35:09 with 6 key names; after the gateway started it was 398 bytes at mtime 21:46:46 with 7. The delta is exactly 80 bytes = 'API_SERVER_KEY=' (15 characters) + 64 hex characters + newline, and the two key-name sets differ by exactly that one name.
env_is_runtime_mutated_by_the_gateway.generate_once_not_per_start: after a full gateway restart the size stayed 398, sha256 unchanged at 635d58bba315269f9df6a3d5149bc931cf0e53a3cd9c33c7a0fbf8e187ccd688, api_server_key_lines=1, duplicate_keys empty and all 7 names present - so .env is stable through the two restarts m05-telegram.sh performs
env_is_runtime_mutated_by_the_gateway.inert: API_SERVER_ENABLED=false and ss -ltn shows only 22, 53 and 5355 before and after - no new listener
env_is_runtime_mutated_by_the_gateway.consequence_for_replication: any .env hash recorded while the gateway is stopped is STALE as soon as it starts, so a replicator comparing the manifest's env_file_sha256 against a running host will see a mismatch that looks like tampering and is not. new_defect_avc_denials.observation: SEVEN enforced denials this boot, all identical: 'avc: denied { lock } for pid=6173 comm="hermes" path="/opt/data/state.db-shm" scontext=system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c519,c720 tcontext=system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c253,c452 tclass=file permissive=0'
new_defect_avc_denials.meaning: the process MCS categories (c519,c720) differ from the file's (c253,c452) and permissive=0 means the lock is genuinely blocked. The path is state.db-shm, SQLite's WAL shared-memory file - the primitive SQLite uses for cross-process locking - so this is state-database machinery, not an incidental file touch.
new_defect_avc_denials.diagnosis: one shared directory is mounted with the EXCLUSIVE relabel by several containers. ':Z' requests a PRIVATE relabel, correct only when a volume belongs to a single container; each container start relabels the tree to its own MCS categories, so the next container finds labels belonging to a previous one. /home/hermes/transport correctly uses ':z' (shared) in both Quadlets, while /home/hermes/gateway-state -> /opt/data uses ':Z' in the gateway Quadlet line 26, provision-openai-key.sh line 61 AND provision-telegram.sh line 66.
new_defect_avc_denials.recurrence: provision-telegram.sh:66 will relabel /opt/data a fourth time at step 8, so the denials will recur unless the option is corrected.
new_defect_avc_denials.impact: the gateway currently works - inference and the tool round trip both passed - so the harm is latent rather than immediate, and the honest statement is that the current observable effect is the denials themselves. But lock denials on state.db-shm are exactly the failure mode that produces intermittent SQLite 'database is locked' / I/O errors and state-persistence failures rather than clean errors, and Phase 7 acceptance explicitly requires 'no new AVC denials', so this must be resolved rather than noted.
new_defect_avc_denials.correct_fix: labelling, not policy. The guide is explicit: investigate AVC denials rather than installing a generated audit2allow module or setting SELinux permissive. Mount the shared state directory with ':z' (shared) in the gateway Quadlet and in both one-shot provisioning scripts, then restart and confirm the denials stop.
